papers.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
papers.authors: Daniel Grimm, Kyra Jongman, Renato Cordeiro Ferreira, Giuseppe Cascavilla et al.
papers.what: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. papers.summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.

papers.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
papers.authors: Thomas Brennan, Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
papers.what: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

papers.title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval
papers.authors: Dayoon Ko, Yichuan Wang, Soyeong Jeong, Joseph E. Gonzalez et al.
papers.what: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. papers.summary: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.

papers.title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
papers.authors: Yifan Jin, Tao Liu
papers.what: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recur
papers.summary: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

papers.title: MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Song Wang, Gongfan Fang et al.
papers.what: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexp
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to $3.58\times$, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

papers.title: Box-conditional Hypothesis Testing for Out-of-Distribution Object Detection
papers.authors: Donghoon Lee, Jusung Park, Shinjin Kang
papers.what: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects is essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of object detectors in real-world deployment. papers.summary: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) objects is essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of object detectors in real-world deployment. We treat the decision on a detected box as a hypothesis test with the null hypothesis that the box covers an object of an in-distribution (ID) class. The null distribution changes with the size of the box and its contact with the image border, and the detector observes both. The test can therefore rank a box only against ID boxes of the same size and border contact, which gives a distribution-free bound on the false-alarm rate for each of them and uncovers the separation that one null distribution hides. The power of the test also rests on the layer it reads. Layers built only for the ID classes have no reason to keep what sets an unknown object apart, so the test reads the features before them. We propose \textbf{PLUM}, a training-free score that pools the last backbone stage inside the box and ranks its distance to the ID classes among ID boxes of the same size and border contact. On the standard benchmark, PLUM reaches the highest AUROC among the compared methods without external models, with 91.5 and 94.5 on PASCAL-VOC and 95.1 and 97.5 on BDD100K. Code: https://github.com/DDOZMI/PLUM

papers.title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
papers.authors: Robin Shing Moon Chan, Ryan Cotterell
papers.what: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves.
papers.summary: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}γ\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

papers.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
papers.authors: Helma Torkamaan, Masoud Mansoury, Yanan Xin, Oscar Oviedo Trespalacios et al.
papers.what: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 res
papers.summary: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

papers.title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
papers.authors: Omer Nezih Gerek
papers.what: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class
papers.summary: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

papers.title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
papers.authors: Mengfan Xu, Zirui Liu, Juan Zhai, Shiqing Ma et al.
papers.what: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed
papers.summary: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.

papers.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
papers.authors: Cole Becker, Taylan Kargin, Kimia Hassibi, Asuman Ozdaglar et al.
papers.what: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discre
papers.summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

papers.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
papers.what: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. papers.summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

papers.title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
papers.authors: Brandon Amos
papers.what: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Je
papers.summary: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

papers.title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
papers.authors: Jianjun Zhou, Hua Geng, Haoyu Guo
papers.what: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencod
papers.summary: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

papers.title: WebThinker: Empowering Large Reasoning Models with Deep Research Capability
papers.authors: Xiaoxi Li, Jiajie Jin, Guanting Dong, Hongjin Qian et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Large reasoning models (LRMs), such as OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1, demonstrate impressive long-horizon reasoning capabilities. However, their reliance on static internal knowledge limits their performance on complex, knowledge-intensive tasks and hinders their ability to produce c
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs), such as OpenAI-o1 and DeepSeek-R1, demonstrate impressive long-horizon reasoning capabilities. However, their reliance on static internal knowledge limits their performance on complex, knowledge-intensive tasks and hinders their ability to produce comprehensive research reports requiring synthesis of diverse web information. To address this, we propose WebThinker, a deep research agent that empowers LRMs to autonomously search the web, navigate among web pages, and draft reports during the reasoning process. WebThinker integrates a Deep Web Explorer module, enabling LRMs to dynamically search, navigate, and extract information from the web when encountering knowledge gaps. It also employs an Autonomous Think-Search-and-Draft strategy, allowing the model to seamlessly interleave reasoning, information gathering, and report writing in real time. To further enhance research tool utilization, we introduce an RL-based training strategy via iterative online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks (GPQA, GAIA, WebWalkerQA, HLE) and scientific report generation tasks (Glaive) demonstrate that WebThinker significantly outperforms existing methods and strong proprietary systems. Our approach enhances LRM reliability and applicability in complex scenarios, paving the way for more capable and versatile deep research systems. The code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/WebThinker.

papers.title: Recognize Anything: A Strong Image Tagging Model
papers.authors: Youcai Zhang, Xinyu Huang, Jinyu Ma, Zhaoyang Li et al.
papers.what: [Conference] We present the Recognize Anything Model (RAM): a strong foundation model for image tagging. RAM makes a substantial step for foundation models in computer vision, demonstrating the zero-shot ability to recognize any common category with high accuracy. By leveraging large-scale im
papers.summary: We present the Recognize Anything Model (RAM): a strong foundation model for image tagging. RAM makes a substantial step for foundation models in computer vision, demonstrating the zero-shot ability to recognize any common category with high accuracy. By leveraging large-scale image-text pairs for training instead of manual annotations, RAM introduces a new paradigm for image tagging.The development of RAM comprises four key steps. Firstly, annotation-free image tags are obtained at scale through automatic text semantic parsing. Subsequently, a preliminary model is trained for automatic annotation by unifying the captioning and tagging tasks, supervised by the original texts and parsed tags, respectively. Thirdly, a data engine is employed to generate additional annotations and clean incorrect ones. Lastly, the model is retrained with the processed data and fine-tuned using a smaller but higher-quality dataset.We evaluate the tagging capability of RAM on numerous benchmarks and observe an impressive zero-shot performance, which significantly outperforms CLIP and BLIP. Remarkably, RAM even surpasses fully supervised models and exhibits a competitive performance compared with the Google tagging API. We have released RAM at https://recognize-anything.github.io/ to foster the advancement of foundation models in computer vision.

papers.title: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models through Visual Contrastive Decoding
papers.authors: Sicong Leng, Hang Zhang, Guanzheng Chen, Xin Shane Li et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have advanced considerably, intertwining visual recognition and language understanding to generate content that is not only coherent but also contextually attuned. Despite their success, LVLMs still suffer from the issue of object hallucinatio
papers.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have advanced considerably, intertwining visual recognition and language understanding to generate content that is not only coherent but also contextually attuned. Despite their success, LVLMs still suffer from the issue of object hallucinations, where models generate plausible yet incorrect outputs that include objects that do not exist in the images. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD), a simple and training-free method that contrasts output distributions derived from original and distorted visual inputs. The proposed VCD effectively reduces the over-reliance on statistical bias and unimodal priors, two essential causes of object hallucinations. This adjustment ensures the generated content is closely grounded to visual inputs, resulting in contextually accurate outputs. Our experiments show that VCD, without either additional training or the usage of external tools, significantly mitigates the object hallucination issue across different LVLM families. Beyond mitigating object hallucinations, VCD also excels in general LVLM benchmarks, highlighting its wide-ranging applicability.

papers.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
papers.authors: Alexandra Souly, Qingyuan Lu, Dillon Bowen, Tu Trinh et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this pro
papers.summary: Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this problem arises because jailbreak researchers lack a standard, high-quality benchmark for evaluating jailbreak performance, leaving researchers to create their own. To create a benchmark, researchers must choose a dataset of forbidden prompts to which a victim model will respond, along with an evaluation method that scores the harmfulness of the victim model's responses. We show that existing benchmarks suffer from significant shortcomings and introduce the StrongREJECT benchmark to address these issues. StrongREJECT's dataset contains prompts that victim models must answer with specific, harmful information, while its automated evaluator measures the extent to which a response gives useful information to forbidden prompts. In doing so, the StrongREJECT evaluator achieves state-of-the-art agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness. Notably, we find that existing evaluation methods significantly overstate jailbreak effectiveness compared to human judgments and the StrongREJECT evaluator. We describe a surprising and novel phenomenon that explains this discrepancy: jailbreaks bypassing a victim model's safety fine-tuning tend to reduce its capabilities. Together, our findings underscore the need for researchers to use a high-quality benchmark, such as StrongREJECT, when developing new jailbreak attacks. We release the StrongREJECT code and data at https://strong-reject.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.

papers.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
papers.authors: Zihan Qiu, Zekun Wang, Bo Zheng, Zeyu Huang et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Gating mechanisms have been widely utilized, from early models like LSTMs and Highway Networks to recent state space models, linear attention, and also softmax attention. Yet, existing literature rarely examines the specific effects of gating. In this work, we conduct comprehensi
papers.summary: Gating mechanisms have been widely utilized, from early models like LSTMs and Highway Networks to recent state space models, linear attention, and also softmax attention. Yet, existing literature rarely examines the specific effects of gating. In this work, we conduct comprehensive experiments to systematically investigate gating-augmented softmax attention variants. Specifically, we perform a comprehensive comparison over 30 variants of 15B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models and 1.7B dense models trained on a 3.5 trillion token dataset. Our central finding is that a simple modification-applying a head-specific sigmoid gate after the Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA)-consistently improves performance. This modification also enhances training stability, tolerates larger learning rates, and improves scaling properties. By comparing various gating positions and computational variants, we attribute this effectiveness to two key factors: (1) introducing non-linearity upon the low-rank mapping in the softmax attention, and (2) applying query-dependent sparse gating scores to modulate the SDPA output. Notably, we find this sparse gating mechanism mitigates 'attention sink' and enhances long-context extrapolation performance, and we also release related $\href{https://github.com/qiuzh20/gated_attention}{codes}$ and $\href{https://huggingface.co/QwQZh/gated_attention}{models}$ to facilitate future research.

papers.title: A Diffusion-Based Framework for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection
papers.authors: Haoyang He, Jiangning Zhang, Hongxu Chen, Xuhai Chen et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Reconstruction-based approaches have achieved remarkable outcomes in anomaly detection. The exceptional image reconstruction capabilities of recently popular diffusion models have sparked research efforts to utilize them for enhanced reconstruction of anomalous images. Nonetheles
papers.summary: Reconstruction-based approaches have achieved remarkable outcomes in anomaly detection. The exceptional image reconstruction capabilities of recently popular diffusion models have sparked research efforts to utilize them for enhanced reconstruction of anomalous images. Nonetheless, these methods might face challenges related to the preservation of image categories and pixel-wise structural integrity in the more practical multi-class setting. To solve the above problems, we propose a Difusion-based Anomaly Detection (DiAD) framework for multi-class anomaly detection, which consists of a pixel-space autoencoder, a latent-space Semantic-Guided (SG) network with a connection to the stable diffusion’s denoising network, and a feature-space pre-trained feature extractor. Firstly, The SG network is proposed for reconstructing anomalous regions while preserving the original image’s semantic information. Secondly, we introduce Spatial-aware Feature Fusion (SFF) block to maximize reconstruction accuracy when dealing with extensively reconstructed areas. Thirdly, the input and reconstructed images are processed by a pre-trained feature extractor to generate anomaly maps based on features extracted at different scales. Experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach which surpasses the state-of-the-art methods, e.g., achieving 96.8/52.6 and 97.2/99.0 (AUROC/AP) for localization and detection respectively on multi-class MVTec-AD dataset. Code will be available at https://lewandofskee.github.io/projects/diad.

papers.title: Gaussian Splatting SLAM
papers.authors: Hidenobu Matsuki, Riku Murai, Paul H. J. Kelly, Andrew J. Davison
papers.what: [Conference] We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. papers.summary: We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. Our method, which runs live at 3fps, utilises Gaussians as the only 3D representation, unifying the required representation for accurate, efficient tracking, mapping, and high-quality rendering. Designed for challenging monocular settings, our approach is seamlessly extendable to RGB-D SLAM when an external depth sensor is available. Several innovations are required to continuously reconstruct 3D scenes with high fidelity from a live camera. First, to move beyond the original 3DGS algorithm, which requires accurate poses from an offline Structure from Motion (SfM) system, we formulate camera tracking for 3DGS using direct optimisation against the 3D Gaussians, and show that this enables fast and robust tracking with a wide basin of convergence. Second, by utilising the explicit nature of the Gaussians, we introduce geometric verification and regularisation to handle the ambiguities occurring in incremental 3D dense reconstruction. Finally, we introduce afull SLAM system which not only achieves state-of-the-art results in novel view synthesis and trajectory estimation but also reconstruction of tiny and even transparent objects.

papers.title: VellSSLH: Sound Type-Guided Selective Speculative Load Hardening for LLVM IR
papers.authors: Swarn Priya
papers.what: [Explore] Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protect
papers.summary: Constant-time cryptographic programs written in C can still leak secrets during speculative execution. Mispredicted branches may allow instructions to access secret data and expose it through observable behavior. Speculative load hardening (SLH) addresses these leaks, but protecting values unnecessarily can introduce significant runtime overhead. We present VellSSLH, which selectively inserts speculative load hardening at LLVM IR. Programmers specify Public and Secret inputs in annotated C programs, and our analysis infers which values may become secret during speculation. The transformation then inserts misspeculation-flag operations and protections only where needed. VellSCT, our extracted checker, validates the resulting LLVM IR. We formalize speculative constant-time (SCT) security by extending Vellvm's LLVM semantics with speculative execution, attacker directives, and leakage observations. Our security type system reasons about SSA joins, symbolic values, poison, pointer provenance, and observable faults, and supports declared declassifications and trusted external services. In Rocq, we prove that programs accepted by the checker satisfy SCT, and that a reference hardening transformation preserves architectural behavior. Evaluated optimized variants are rechecked for SCT but are not covered by this preservation proof. Our mechanized guarantees apply at LLVM IR; security of the generated binary additionally depends on backend and hardware assumptions. We evaluate VellSSLH on 24 cryptographic entries on a bare-metal Intel processor. VellSSLH achieves 4.03% lower geometric-mean runtime than LLVM SLH, with 13 comparisons favoring VellSSLH, eight favoring LLVM SLH, and three inconclusive. For X25519, VellSSLH improves runtime by 22.69% over LLVM SLH with only 1.86% overhead over unprotected code. Compared with Ultimate SLH, VellSSLH achieves 19.65% lower runtime.

papers.authors: Haochen Yang, Zhuoran Gao, Geqing Tao, Yusi Dong et al.
papers.what: [Explore] High-pressure job interviews induce anxiety and impair performance. Existing mock training suffers from a trade-off among cost, standardization, and physical presence. This study investigated how a robot interviewer's verbal persona (supportive vs. challenging) and nonverbal back
papers.summary: High-pressure job interviews induce anxiety and impair performance. Existing mock training suffers from a trade-off among cost, standardization, and physical presence. This study investigated how a robot interviewer's verbal persona (supportive vs. challenging) and nonverbal backchanneling (active vs. negative) affect users' psychological states and facial expressions in a simulated interview. In a 2x2 between-subjects experiment (N=28), participants interacted with a NAO robot. Subjective measures (state anxiety, self-efficacy, social presence) and objective facial emotion recognition were collected. Results showed that a supportive persona reduced task load, increased perceived robot warmth and mind perception, and decreased perceived surveillance and robot discomfort. Active backchanneling increased non-neutral (p = .021) and anxiety-tension facial affect (p = .048). A significant interaction effect between persona and backchanneling was found on social presence (p = .045). The subjective-objective consistency was 67.9%, indicating complementary measurement modalities. The findings provide preliminary support for the social buffering hypothesis in human-robot interaction.

papers.title: Quadratic APN Functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with a Self-Equivalence of Prime Order
papers.authors: Emanuele Bellini

papers.summary: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ have the lowest possible differential uniformity. The only known APN permutation in even dimension, in dimension six, is equivalent to a quadratic APN function with a nontrivial linear self-equivalence; no APN permutation is known for even $n \geq 8$. In a published collection of about 3.8 million quadratic APN classes of dimension eight, at most 0.34% have a nontrivial linear self-equivalence. In dimension ten, the 25 literature classes considered here all have one. We study all quadratic APN functions of $\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with such a self-equivalence, which usually confines them to a much smaller linear space. Up to conjugacy and power similarity, self-equivalences of prime order have 299 types. We settle 298 of them. Elementary lemmas exclude 280 types, and exhaustive searches confirm this for 242 of them. The other 18 types are settled by exhaustive searches with exact equivalence certificates. Up to extended affine equivalence, the 298 types contain 29 classes of quadratic APN functions, four of them new. This also classifies the quadratic APN functions with coefficients in a subfield. Exactly 24 classes contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_4$, and all 3 that contain one with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_{32}$ are among them. The open type consists of the quadratic canonical triplicate functions. They correspond to maximum additive Hermitian rank-distance codes. Three different searches find only the invariants of 16 classes, all among the 29. We conjecture there are no others. No quadratic APN function in the 298 settled types is Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev equivalent to a permutation.

papers.title: Broken Adaptive Ridge in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressions
papers.authors: Gianluca Cubadda, Luca Margaritella, Orest Prifti
papers.what: [Explore] We study regularized estimation in high-dimensional vector autoregressions under physical dependence and row-wise approximate sparsity using the Broken Adaptive Ridge (BAR) estimator. papers.summary: We study regularized estimation in high-dimensional vector autoregressions under physical dependence and row-wise approximate sparsity using the Broken Adaptive Ridge (BAR) estimator. BAR is an iteratively reweighted Ridge procedure whose fixed-point first-order conditions imply a coordinatewise thresholding rule that produces exact zeros. We show that the BAR estimation error can be analyzed on the union of the population support above the BAR threshold and the support selected in the sample. The size of this union can be controlled at the rate implied by approximate sparsity, allowing us to establish the required restricted-curvature condition and derive L1, L2, and prediction error rates when the number of regressors grows polynomially with the sample size and may exceed it. Under exact sparsity, the resulting rates recover the familiar rates for sparse high-dimensional estimation. Monte Carlo experiments across a range of high-dimensional VAR designs show that BAR delivers strong estimation and forecasting performance, and retains a high share of relevant coefficients relative to Lasso, adaptive Lasso, and SCAD. An application to U.S. inflation forecasting using FRED-MD shows particularly strong performance at the one-month horizon.

papers.title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference
papers.authors: Elena Dal Torrione, Chan Park, Laura Forastiere
papers.what: [Explore] Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance,
papers.summary: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.

papers.summary: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.

papers.title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
papers.authors: Xiaochen Zhang, Wenjing Zheng, Xingye Kang, Vamsi Manthena
papers.what: [Explore] Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this
papers.summary: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Threshold Designated-Verifier Digital Signatures for Resource-Constrained Devices
papers.authors: Andrew Wright, Aydin Abadi, Ittoop Vergheese Puthoor
papers.what: [Explore] Digital signatures are synonymous with data integrity and authenticity. Among applications such as e-commerce, software distribution, and instruction processing they play a vital role in the secure communication of data. Within this context and in preparation for quantum adversar
papers.summary: Digital signatures are synonymous with data integrity and authenticity. Among applications such as e-commerce, software distribution, and instruction processing they play a vital role in the secure communication of data. Within this context and in preparation for quantum adversarial tactics we present three new information-theoretic threshold designated verifier digital signature schemes and prove them secure against \textit{any} adversary under the standard security criterion. The $n$-of-$n$ multi-signature, $t$-of-$n$ threshold with dealer, and $t$-of-$n$ threshold without dealer designated verifier signature schemes can be implemented with simple mathematical constructs and we demonstrate the efficiency of these with evaluation of signature computation ($\lessapprox$ 80\,ms) and verification times ($\lessapprox$ 150\,ms) on the resource constrained platform of Raspberry Pi 4. We find our scheme also has equivalent or improved (2$\times$) performance than a comparable state-of-the-art post-quantum threshold digital signature scheme on both resource constrained devices and the more capable consumer-grade 2025 M5 MacBook Pro.

papers.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
papers.authors: Junjie Xiao, Renaud Lambiotte, Hiroshi Kori
papers.what: [Explore] In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's
papers.summary: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

papers.title: CS-MPC: Contraction-Certified Sampling-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems Under Uncertainty
papers.authors: Yashwanth Kumar Nakka
papers.what: [Explore] We present contraction-certified sampling-based model predictive control (CS-MPC) for tracking and safety of nonlinear robotic systems under parametric uncertainty, disturbances, and safety constraints that are revealed online. CS-MPC uses a contraction-certified tracking feedbac
papers.summary: We present contraction-certified sampling-based model predictive control (CS-MPC) for tracking and safety of nonlinear robotic systems under parametric uncertainty, disturbances, and safety constraints that are revealed online. CS-MPC uses a contraction-certified tracking feedback inside every sampled rollout, which concentrates the rollouts around the reference, and an execution layer that verifies the applied input using a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier function condition. We derive a verification procedure for nonlinear contraction of the feedback-closed dynamics, and we prove a finite-sample stochastic stability bound and a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee. We validate CS-MPC in simulation on a rover, a quadrotor, and an asteroid landing. When compared with standard model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, CS-MPC attains the same tracking error with 7 to 20 times fewer rollouts for the rover, and a 2 to 4 times lower tracking error for the quadrotor, with no safety violations in 200 Monte Carlo missions.

papers.title: What a Memory Preview Cannot Tell You: Ambiguity in AI Memory Permissions
papers.authors: Sadia Noman Tonni, Nafis Fuad Shahid
papers.what: [Explore] A memory rule states when an assistant may reuse a remembered event, and an editor can confirm a rule by previewing one use it allows and one it blocks. papers.summary: A memory rule states when an assistant may reuse a remembered event, and an editor can confirm a rule by previewing one use it allows and one it blocks. We ask what such a preview lets a person infer about the rule they saved. For an editor with six or twelve valid rules, we enumerate every rule compatible with a preview. Splitting the rules most evenly does not target the question a user cares about. For an explicit preference, two adaptive tests leave all three recommendation scopes open (for a one-off choice the outcome turns on a tie), while one test of transfer to another task settles the question. Weak previews are also the default. Under the intended rule, 36 of 39 possible allowed/blocked pairs contain a blocked example that no rule allows, and no pair identifies the rule. Three or four tests suffice here; when permissions depend on each other, a fixed checklist grows to six or nine and adaptive questioning needs at most five or seven. These counts use a specified rule vocabulary and fictional events. In a small pilot, 10 of 20 people who saw such a weak preview of a rule they had just chosen mispredicted, or were unsure about, at least one of two uses, and none of those 10 said the outcomes matched what they wanted. Whether better previews help people is untested.

papers.title: Random Utility Models in the Consumption-Budget Setting: Vertex and Network-Flow Characterizations
papers.authors: Haoge Chang, Kota Saito, Mingxi Zhu
papers.what: [Explore] This note supplements our paper \textit{Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations} and serves two purposes: 1. We clarify the conceptual distinctions between two classes of random utility mod
papers.summary: This note supplements our paper \textit{Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations} and serves two purposes: 1. We clarify the conceptual distinctions between two classes of random utility models (RUM): those in the consumption-budget setting \citep{kitamura2019nonparametric} (hereafter KS) and those in the finite-alternative setting (e.g., Chapter~7 of \cite{chambers2016revealed}). In particular, we show (Theorem 1) that each rational type, as defined in KS, can be obtained as a coordinate projection of the deterministic choice vector induced by a strict preference ranking that satisfies what we call a patch-monotonicity condition. 2. We generalize the network-flow characterization for finite-alternative RUM in \cite{fiorini2004short} to the consumption-budget setting (Theorem 2). Specifically, we show that a vector of choice probabilities in the consumption-budget setting is rationalizable in the KS sense if and only if it is the image of a unit flow on a multi-arc powerset digraph under a fixed linear map. The key distinction is that our digraph allows multiple arcs between the same pair of nodes, whereas the digraph in Fiorini has at most one arc between any pair of nodes.

papers.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
papers.authors: Hua Yang, Aditya Bhardwaj, Shidong Pan, Bowen Xu
papers.what: [Explore] Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present Privac
papers.summary: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.

papers.title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners
papers.authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair i
papers.summary: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.

papers.title: In Situ Monitoring and Predictive Modeling of Harmful Algal Blooms with Autonomous Surface Vehicles
papers.authors: Nenyi Kweku Nkensen Dadson, Jean Paul Gonzalez, Daniel P. Arabie, Ryan J. Cedel et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs) pose significant environmental, economic, and public-health challenges in coastal and inland water bodies, creating a need for scalable methods to collect spatially distributed water-quality data. This paper presents an autonomous surface vessel-based
papers.summary: Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs) pose significant environmental, economic, and public-health challenges in coastal and inland water bodies, creating a need for scalable methods to collect spatially distributed water-quality data. This paper presents an autonomous surface vessel-based sensing system for in-situ water-quality monitoring related to harmful algal bloom detection. The system integrates a BlueBoat Autonomous Surface Vessel (ASV), a motorized winch for depth-controlled sonde deployment, a multiparameter water-quality sonde, side-scan sonar, and an event-camera payload. Autonomous waypoint missions were used to collect measurements across selected sampling regions and multiple depths, enabling both horizontal and vertical characterization of environmental conditions. Field deployments were conducted in Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana, with additional measurements collected in False River, Louisiana to increase dataset diversity. The collected measurements included algal pigment indicators, nutrient concentration, turbidity, temperature, and other water-quality parameters relevant to bloom formation. In addition, complementary sonar and event-camera data were collected during vehicle operation to provide contextual environmental information. A machine-learning classification approach was also evaluated using the collected water-quality measurements to support HAB and non-HAB classification. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using a modular ASV platform for repeatable, multi-modal water-quality data collection and support future development of autonomous monitoring systems.

papers.title: On the Same Track: Privacy Leaks in Electric Rail Transport via Magnetic Fields
papers.authors: Stefan Czybik, Pia Hanfeld, Konrad Rieck
papers.what: [Explore] Inertial sensors of smartphones are a well-known privacy risk, as they allow inferring sensitive user movements and activity without explicit permissions. Among these sensors, the magnetometer has received little attention, as it is assumed to measure mainly the Earth's magnetic
papers.summary: Inertial sensors of smartphones are a well-known privacy risk, as they allow inferring sensitive user movements and activity without explicit permissions. Among these sensors, the magnetometer has received little attention, as it is assumed to measure mainly the Earth's magnetic field. In this paper, we show that electric trains generate distinctive magnetic fields that can be captured by a smartphone magnetometer. Apps deployed on the device can access these signals without user permission, enabling two novel attacks on passenger privacy: First, we are able to determine whether the user is riding an electric train (transport mode detection). Second, we can infer whether other victims are aboard the same train due to shared patterns in the magnetic field (colocation prediction). In an empirical evaluation across 217 train rides, we demonstrate that both attacks are effective, confirming a real-world threat. We discuss countermeasures and argue that magnetometer access should require explicit user permission in mobile operating systems.

papers.authors: Stanisław M. S. Halkiewicz
papers.what: [Explore] Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. papers.summary: Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. Under a local treatment-effect drift, the statistic for the equally weighted treated-cell effect has worst-case mean shift $(c/q)Γ$, where $Γ=\sqrt{N_1}\|w-u\|_2$ is design-only and $q$ is the cluster-score noise scale. Projection matches the exposure to cohort, event-time, additive, and saturated group-time pilots; when residualized treatment is constant within treated group-time cells, $Γ_{\mathrm{gt}}=Γ$. A direct score estimator is feasible with fixed panel length as clusters grow. Because a debiased quadratic pilot is nonregular at zero, we use two regular one-sided procedures: a reverse-triangle multiplier lower bound to detect unsafe envelopes and covariance-aware noncentral-$χ^2$ inversion to certify adequacy. At $5\%$ nominal size with a five-point tolerance, the shift threshold is $0.652$. In the Callaway--Sant'Anna minimum-wage panel, where every treated-cell weight is positive, the saturated $95\%$ lower shift bound is $0.793$, so conventional inference is not uniformly certified. A complementary Brazilian property-tax reanalysis with $2{,}840$ municipalities withholds certification in all four classes; its smallest lower bound is $1.040$. Under the maintained many-cluster approximation, castle-doctrine homicide passes for additive cohort-plus-event-time heterogeneity with a $95\%$ upper bound of $0.236$; its saturated covariance lacks one required rank. Divorce is inconclusive. These envelopes are not predictions of realized rejection. The diagnostic separates point correction, uniform exposure, and statistically warranted certification.

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.authors: Mateusz Wozniak, Qi Gao, Agnieszka Wykowska
papers.what: [Explore] Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human v
papers.summary: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

papers.title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care
papers.authors: Thalia Viranda, Shupeng Wang, Jia Bo, Yuchen Yang et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering
papers.summary: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering evidence-based interventions, and how to manage personal-data use and sharing across AI and care stakeholders. We designed and evaluated ARC, a voice-based conversational agent that operationalizes multidomain lifestyle intervention through sessions with predefined goals, participant context, and evidence-based components. In a 3-day remote study, 80 older adults completed 473 sessions across six session types (9,183 turns; averaging 19.4 turns and 6 minutes per session). Participants reported favorable usability, acceptability, and use intentions. System-level analyses showed strong domain-level but modest participant-specific contextual reuse, no significant personalization-fidelity association, and fidelity limitations centered on incomplete delivery of intervention components rather than off-protocol drift. Within care relationships, expectations for personal-data use and sharing varied by data type and recipient. Our findings support feasibility of conversational delivery of multidomain lifestyle intervention, offer methods and system-design insights for longitudinal evaluation, and motivate an evaluation agenda for generative AI health interventions: user-experience and outcome measures should be complemented by evidence of whether intended intervention processes were delivered as designed.
